key_insight: A submitted solution that closely matches LLM output does not reliably reveal how much mathematical thinking a student offloaded.
engineering_relevance: Educational AI tools should support process-level analysis of student–LLM interactions rather than infer cognitive engagement from final-answer similarity alone.
method: Followed first-year linear algebra students across three differently designed homework tasks.
Interpreted prompts as regulatory events using self-regulated learning and choice-affluent environments.
Compared chatlogs with submitted solutions and identified five interaction structures.
evidence_signal: The study analyzed 429 prompts across 59 chatlogs from 23 students; 10 of the 15 who completed all three tasks changed their dominant interaction structure.
watch_item: The small, course-specific sample limits generalization, and prompt traces do not directly measure all student thinking.
paper_title: What the submission does not show: Complexifying cognitive offloading in students' mathematical work with LLMs
